The evidence across multiple sources consistently indicates that hamburger menus are generally bad for user engagement, though context matters. Empirical testing by Spotify showed that replacing the hamburger menu with a tab bar led to users clicking 9% more in general and 30% more on actual menu items [d1][d6], and Facebook similarly saw greater engagement after switching to bottom navigation [d4]. A study by the Nielsen Norman Group found that hiding main navigation via a hamburger menu cuts discoverability "almost in half," increases task time, and raises perceived task difficulty [d5]; the Zeebox app also saw engagement numbers halved after adopting a hamburger menu [d5]. UX researchers identify several structural reasons for these outcomes: the menu hides options by default (lower discoverability), forces extra taps (higher interaction cost), clashes with platform navigation patterns, and is not glanceable [d3][d4]. Major companies including Facebook, Google, Apple, YouTube, and Microsoft have abandoned the hamburger menu in recognition of its negative impact on user engagement [d2]. That said, one source notes there are instances where the hamburger menu is an appropriate choice, particularly in contexts where exposing users to new content is not the primary goal — meaning a visible central menu is better for many but not all sites [d7].
